Spine motion restriction

Previously it was called cervical spine immobilization and since true immobilization of the spine is unattainable, that is why spine motion restriction term was used instead

Spine motion restriction (SMR) is the maneuver done to reduce movement in a patient’s spine in trauma victims, thereby preventing spinal cord injury in a potentially unstable spine => preventing disability

Sgt. David Bedard, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

Spine motion restriction is achieved by applying a rigid cervical collar, rigid extrication device (for extrication), long back board (also for extrication) and a gurney with appropriate straps and sandbags for stabilization

Alexisrael, CC BY-SA 3.0 , via Wikimedia Commons

Spine motion restriction can be done manually by an emergency provider by applying hands to the both sides of the head into the neck to stabilize the c spine of the patient

If the patient on cervical collar need airway management, then the collar is removed and head is stabilized manually and airway management is done and then the collar put back again

SMR indications

Any altered mental status (GCS < 15) => patient is confused or AMS then needs SMR, Pediatric patients may demonstrate altered mental status with agitation , apnea , hypopnea or somnolescence

Focal neurological signs and/or symptoms (e.g. weakness , tingling or numbness)

Midline neck or back pain and/ or tenderness, painful rotation/tilt of the neck

Anatomic deformity of the spine

Unreliable patient interaction including distraction with a painful injury or distressing circumstances

Communication/ language barrier that prevent accurate assessment

Lack of cooperation or contribution during exam

High energy trauma mechanisms: Axial load injuries (diving injuries , spearing tackles) , sudden acceleration/ deceleration injuries, lateral bending forces to neck/ torso

65 years of age or older

Equipment

Adjustable rigid cervical collar

Short, rigid extrication device

X-ray translucent long back board for extrication

Soft padding placed where there is contact between skin and devices mentioned

Gurney with appropriate straps for stabilization of the patient

Procedure

1- Assess airway and manage the airway if it need to be managed while maintaining manual SMR

2- Do a pre SMR assessment of the motor, sensory and circulatory examination and document it

3- Place the rigid cervical collar and adjust size

4- If patient can self extricate then assist them in getting into the gurney but if not then extrication is required, extrication device is used as needed to move the patient to gurney Then, it is removed by log roll

5- Secure the patient to the gurney with straps in a supine position, if supine position can’t be tolerated then position of comfort is done, if patient is obviously pregnant then left lateral position is preferred

6- Do a post SMR assessment of the motor, sensory and circulatory examination and document it

Contraindications

Bleeding that is can’t be controlled with the SMR in place

Uncontrolled vomiting because SMR risk airway patency

Notes

Effort should be made to diagnose or exclude the spine injury and remove the patient from this form of rigid device as soon as possible (because it is not comfortable for the patient)

Rigid backboards use is limited to extrication and transfer of patients to a gurney, because their prolonged use may induce pain, agitation, respiratory compromise and lead to pressure ulcers

SMR is performed with the patient supine, it cannot be safely performed with a patient in a sitting position

If elevation of the head is required, maintain alignment of the neck and torso while elevating the head consider reverse Trendelenburg, if stretcher allows

Saltanat ebli, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons

Children may require additional padding under the shoulders to avoid excessive cervical spine flexion with SMR
